title: Blacksmiths? You got that right!
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a book pre-order plug and banter about watching blacksmithing videos. They trace the name "blacksmith" (hammer scale or iron's dark color), the role of blacksmiths in communities and armies, and farriers who shoed horses. The hosts cover the Bronze Age and Iron Age, early iron from meteorites, bloomeries, blast furnaces, pig iron, and wrought iron, plus water-powered hammers. They explain iron types by carbon content (wrought iron, steel, cast iron), quenching, and steel's history. Tools are covered next: forge fuels (charcoal, coal, coke, gas), the anvil and its horn, hardy hole, pritchel hole, and tongs. Techniques follow: heat colors from white hot to red hot, forge welding with flux, scarf welds, drawing, upsetting, peening, bending and twisting, and hand-forged nail making. The episode ends with a listener mail about being an Olympic torch bearer and the torch kiss handoff, then a sign-off.

entities.name: Stuff You Should Know: An Incomplete Compendium of Mostly Interesting Things

segments.title: Book plug and blacksmithing video banter
segments.summary: Josh plugs the new book and the hosts open with banter about watching blacksmithing videos, including a bearded axe video and the appeal of smiths.

segments.title: Origin of the name blacksmith
segments.summary: The hosts explain that blacksmiths were named for working iron, with theories about hammer scale and iron's dark color. They note that Smith is a very common surname derived from the trade.

segments.title: Blacksmiths' role in communities and armies
segments.summary: Blacksmiths were essential to every community and to armies, making weapons, armor, and repairing gear. Apprentices helped them, and communities could stall if one was sick.

segments.title: Farriers and horseshoeing
segments.summary: Blacksmiths became more specialized, and farriers made horseshoes fitted to each horse's hoof. Farriers kept working after blacksmithing declined.

segments.title: Bronze Age and the start of metalworking
segments.summary: Early tools were stone. Bronze, made from copper and tin, had a low melting point and could be cast in molds, and it defined an era. The hosts note the Iron Age was a period of cultural decline in its early centuries.

segments.title: Early iron: meteorites, bloom and bloomeries
segments.summary: Early iron came from meteorites and was rare, prized even above gold. The Chalybes are said to have learned to mine iron ore. Early smiths made bloom in bloomeries, which removed some impurities but left slag.

segments.title: Blast furnaces, pig iron and wrought iron
segments.summary: Larger furnaces with bellows reached hotter temperatures to produce pig iron. Pig iron was then hammered to remove slag and make wrought iron. The hosts say water-powered hammers may have been developed after the thirteenth-century plague.

segments.title: Types of iron: wrought iron, steel, cast iron
segments.summary: Iron types are defined by carbon content. Wrought iron has low carbon and silicate fibers. Steel has more carbon, forming a harder structure. Cast iron is high carbon, brittle, and formed by casting. Quenching is discussed, along with early steel-making by intuition.

segments.title: Forge, anvil and hand tools
segments.summary: The hosts describe the forge, tongs, and gloves. They cover the anvil's horn, face, and step, the pritchel hole and hardy hole, and how tools fit the hardy hole. The anvil is mounted on a buried tree stump.

segments.title: Forge fuels and safety
segments.summary: Blacksmiths historically used charcoal, then coal, with coke as a purer fuel. Gas forges are common now. The hosts discuss ventilation and protective gear like leather aprons.

segments.title: Heat colors, forge welding and techniques
segments.summary: Iron color indicates temperature, from red hot to white hot. Black Bear Forge is shown making chain with scarf welds and flux. Other techniques include drawing, upsetting, peening, and bending and twisting with square bars.

segments.title: Hand-forged nails and wrap-up
segments.summary: Nail making is described as labor-intensive. The hosts close with a note that they may have gotten details wrong, and recommend watching videos.
